answers.question: What stages does the executable patch-validation funnel in Li et al. use to judge a generated patch?
answers.answer: The funnel has five ordered gates, running from answer availability to executable repair: (1) Usable: the response has a parseable patch-like answer that can enter patch extraction. (2) Applied: the extracted patch changes the target source and applies to the vulnerable checkout. (3) Compiled: the patched project builds far enough for validation to proceed. (4) PoV pass: the vulnerability-specific proof-of-vulnerability trigger is blocked. (5) Full validation pass: the patch also passes the broader validation suite available for the Vul4J project.

answers.question: What three kinds of components make up the safety circuit that Chu et al. describe?
answers.answer: The safety circuit has three kinds of components: Harmful Detection Heads, which respond to harmful inputs; Safety Neurons, which mediate and stabilize safety signals in the residual stream; and Refusal Heads, which translate these signals into safe response generation.

answers.question: What task and setting do Musaffar et al. use to study adversarial intent in human-AI teams?
answers.answer: They use a 25-round trivia game played by three human agents and a malicious AI manipulator. The AI follows a model-based reinforcement learning policy to manipulate trust and degrade team performance. An LLM-based observer reads only behavioral traces (chat logs, agent selections, trust allocations) and classifies whether the AI's behavior is adversarial. It doesn't see the trivia questions, answer options, or ground-truth answers, so the task is task-agnostic.

answers.question: How does CoCoTen build and decompose its co-occurrence tensor, including window size and decomposition rank?
answers.answer: CoCoTen builds a windowed co-occurrence matrix for each prompt, using a sliding window (typically 5–10 tokens) over the entire corpus vocabulary, giving N×N matrices. With M prompts, these are stacked into an N×N×M tensor X built from both jailbreak and benign prompts. The tensor is then decomposed with CP (CANDECOMP/PARAFAC) decomposition into a sum of R rank-one tensors, producing factor matrices A (N×R), B (N×R) and C (M×R). C serves as the embeddings matrix of the prompts. In experiments, window sizes of 3, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 and ranks of 1, 10, 30, 50 and 80 were explored. The main results use a window size of 5 and a rank of 10.

answers.question: What is defensive refusal bias, and how often do aligned models refuse legitimate cyber-defense requests, according to Campbell et al.?
answers.answer: Defensive Refusal Bias is the tendency of safety-tuned frontier LLMs to refuse assistance for authorized defensive cybersecurity tasks when those tasks include language similar to an offensive cyber task. Across all 2,390 NCCDC conversations, the overall refusal rate was 12.2% (291 refusals). It varied by model: 19.5% for the safety-focused model, 10.2% for the frontier model and 6.6% for the open-source model. Prompts with offensive-sounding terms were refused at 30.5%, versus 11.2% for semantically equivalent prompts without them (2.72×).

answers.question: Where was the OR-Bench over-refusal benchmark published, and what does it measure?
answers.answer: OR-Bench was published in the Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Vancouver, Canada, PMLR 267, 2025. It measures over-refusal in LLMs, meaning how often models reject innocuous (safe) prompts and become less helpful because of safety alignment. It has 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 categories, a hard subset of about 1,000 prompts, and 600 toxic prompts that check models don't respond indiscriminately. It was used to evaluate 32 LLMs across 8 model families.
